title: Dana 30 Front Axle — Service and Upgrade Path (YJ)

parts.name: Ball joint set (upper + lower, both sides)
Inner axle seals + unit bearing (per side)

citations.title: Spicer/Dana 30 axle service specifications (Jeep front)
Jeep YJ FSM — front axle U-joint and ball joint service

summary: The Dana 30 front under a YJ is a capable, well-supported axle that handles 31s easily and 33s with care. Most "front axle" problems are wear items: clicking U-joints, sloppy ball joints, and leaking seals — all serviceable in a driveway. The Dana 30 only becomes the weak link past 35-inch tires or hard rock use, at which point you regear, add a locker, and upgrade shafts rather than swap the housing. Budget $60 for a U-joint, up to ~$1,500 if you regear and lock it.
description:
The high-pinion Dana 30 is the front axle in every YJ. It is not a heavy-duty axle, but it is plentiful, cheap to service, and strong enough for the tire sizes most YJs run. The key is to treat the wear items before they cause trouble: a worn front U-joint or ball joint shows up as steering wander, clunking, and uneven tire wear, and a neglected one can leave you stranded with a locked-up front hub.

A **clicking sound on full lock** is the classic worn front-axle U-joint — the closed-knuckle Dana 30 uses a U-joint inside the knuckle as the steering/drive joint. Replace them in pairs with non-greaseable Spicer joints (the solid caps last longer than greaseable ones in this application). **Ball joints** wear and cause wander and death-wobble contributions; check for play with the tire off the ground and replace upper and lower as a set, then get an alignment. **Inner axle seals** weep gear oil into the inner knuckle — replace the seal and the unit/hub bearing together while you are in there.

For 31s and most 33-inch builds, a healthy Dana 30 with good joints is plenty. It starts to show its limits past 33s, under repeated hard rock impacts, or when paired with a front locker that puts full torque through both shafts. The upgrade path, in order of value: regear to match your tires (4.56 for 33s), add a selectable locker or limited-slip, and step up to chromoly axle shafts and U-joints if you break stock parts. A full housing swap (Dana 44 or aftermarket) is the last step and only worth it on a serious 37-inch build.

Pull the wheel, caliper, and rotor/hub, then the unit bearing and stub shaft. The U-joint comes out of the inner axle with a press or a vise and sockets — support the yoke ears so you do not crack them. New ball joints want a ball-joint press and proper torque. Reassemble with fresh seals, set hub bearing preload per the unit-bearing spec, refill the differential, and align the front end afterward.
pros: Cheap, plentiful, and fully serviceable in a home driveway
Strong enough for 31s and most 33-inch YJ builds
Clear upgrade path (gears, locker, shafts) before any housing swap
cons: Closed-knuckle U-joints and ball joints are real wear items — inspect them
Becomes the weak link past 35s or under a hard front locker
A neglected front U-joint can fail and lock the hub on the trail

title: The Dana 35 Rear: Live With It or Upgrade

citations.title: Jeep axle reference — List of Jeep axles
Yukon Dana 35 upgrade catalog

summary: Every YJ left the factory with a Dana 35 rear, and it is the platform's known weak link. On 31s with a daily-driven truck it is fine. On 33s with a locker and a heavy right foot, the c-clip shafts snap and the tubes bend. Whether you upgrade depends honestly on how you use the truck.
description:
The straight answer: if you run 31" tires, drive the YJ on the street and mild trails, and do not have a rear locker, the Dana 35 will live — keep it, and put your money into springs and steering. The failure mode is predictable: it breaks under shock load with traction (a locked rear on 33s climbing a ledge), and because it uses c-clip axle shafts, a broken shaft can leave the wheel and tire behind you on the trail.

If you are building past 33s, locking the rear, or wheeling hard, the Dana 35 becomes a liability and the question is repair-tier versus replace-tier. Repair-tier: chromoly or RCV shafts and a c-clip eliminator address the shaft failure and the wheel-loss risk for a few hundred dollars, and a Grizzly/Detroit locker handles traction. That keeps a 35 alive for a moderate 33" build. Replace-tier: swap to a Ford 8.8 (cheap, strong, disc brakes, same width family with the right shafts) or a Dana 44 — the real answer for a 35"+ rock truck.

While the axle is apart for any of this, regear both ends to match your tires — 4.10 for 31s, 4.56 for 33s on the 4.0L. Regearing only the rear is never an option; the front Dana 30 must match exactly.
steps: Identify your rear: all factory YJ rears are Dana 35 c-clip — confirm the cover shape and ratio tag.
For a keep-it build: install chromoly shafts + a c-clip eliminator and a locker.
For a replace build: source a Ford 8.8 or Dana 44 of the correct width and shaft pattern.
Regear front and rear to the same ratio for your tire size.
Have a shop set up the gears unless you own the tools and a dial indicator — gear setup is unforgiving.

title: YJ Tub and Footwell Rust Repair

parts.name: Front floor pan / footwell patch panels (pair)

citations.title: Key Parts / Classic 2 Current — YJ floor and body panel catalog
Jeep YJ rust-repair writeups (footwell and rear corners)

summary: Every old YJ rusts in the same places: the front footwells under the pedals, the rear floor by the wheel wells, the seat-belt mounts, and the lower rear corners. Surface rust you can treat and seal; perforated metal at the footwells or seat-belt mounts is a safety and structural repair that needs cut-and-weld patch panels. Budget $60 for a localized seal-up, up to $1,500 in panels and consumables for a full floor. Do not bondo over rusted-through footwells — water gets in through the windshield and top, and a soft floor near the seat-belt anchors is dangerous.
description:
YJs are open-top Jeeps that live outside and take in water through the windshield seal, the soft-top seams, and the body drains. That water pools in the footwells and rear floor and rusts the tub from the inside out. The good news is that the YJ tub is bolted to the frame and reproduction panels are widely available, so even a badly rusted floor is repairable without replacing the whole body.

Pull the carpet, seats, and seat belts and inspect with a screwdriver or wire wheel. Press on the footwells, the floor under the seat-belt anchors, the rear floor by the wheel arches, and the lower body corners — anything that flexes or flakes through is a patch job. Common YJ rust zones are the front driver and passenger footwells, the rear floor/wheel-well seams, the seat-belt and seat-mount areas, and the rocker/lower corners. Map every spot now so you cut once.

**Surface rust** that has not gone through gets wire-wheeled to clean metal, treated with a rust converter, primed, and sealed. **Perforated metal** — especially at footwells and seat-belt mounts — must be cut out and replaced with a welded patch panel; sealant or fiberglass over a structural hole is not a repair. Reproduction floor pans, footwell patches, and rear corners are available and largely pre-formed, which makes the welding straightforward if you can run a clean MIG bead on thin metal.

Cut back to solid metal, fit the patch with weld-through primer on the mating flanges, and stitch-weld to avoid warping the thin sheet. Grind, seam-seal every joint, prime, and paint. Undercoat the underside and treat the inside of the tub so the repair lasts. Reinstall with fresh body-mount bushings if they are crushed, and make sure the body drains are clear so water leaves instead of pooling again. Seat-belt anchor areas must be welded to solid structure — this is a safety-critical detail, not cosmetic.
pros: Reproduction panels make even a bad YJ floor fully repairable
The tub bolts off the frame, so access for welding is good
Fixing it right protects the seat-belt mounts and resale value
cons: Perforated footwells need welding skill, not filler
It is dirty, time-consuming work that often grows once you open it up
Skipping the drains and sealing means the rust comes right back

title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement

parts.name: PowerStop Z16 Autospecialty front kit (pads + rotors)

citations.title: PowerStop Z16 brake kit application — 91-99 YJ/TJ
Quadratec YJ brake drums and rotors catalog

summary: Pop the wheel, pull the two 13mm slide bolts, lift the caliper out of the bracket, swap pads, compress the piston with a C-clamp, then unbolt the bracket from the knuckle, slide the rotor off the hub, and reverse — about 90 minutes for both fronts on a YJ.
description:
Front brakes on a YJ are stopped-clock straightforward: single-piston floating caliper, vented rotor, two pad shims, two slide pins. The 1987–1989 trucks use a smaller rotor and caliper than the 1990+ trucks, which got the heavier brake setup that ran through every TJ and most XJs. Pads and rotors are wear items — replace pads when there's 3mm of friction material left, replace rotors any time you replace pads if the rotor is below minimum thickness (stamped on the hub face) or has hard scoring you can feel with a fingernail.

Treat this job with respect — brakes are not where you cut corners or hurry. Use jack stands on the frame rails, not on the axle (the axle moves up when you remove the wheel and weight). Pump the brake pedal once after reassembly and before you move the truck to push the pads against the rotor; if you skip this, your first stop has no brakes. Then drive 10–15 mph in an empty lot and do a few firm stops to bed the new pads — this transfers a thin layer of friction material onto the rotor face, which is what actually does the stopping.

Compressing the piston pushes brake fluid backward through the line and up into the master cylinder reservoir. Open the reservoir cap and remove a few ounces of fluid before you compress, or it'll overflow when you push the piston in. A C-clamp with the old pad as a pad-saver works fine; a proper caliper compressor tool is faster but $25 you don't need to spend. While the rotor is off, take 60 seconds with a wire brush to clean the hub face — rust between the hub and the rotor is what causes that pulsating brake pedal six months later.

Brand math: PowerStop's Z16 kit at around $120 gets you pads and rotors that exceed factory performance and run cooler than the OEM Mopar units. Bosch QuietCast ceramic pads on Raybestos Professional rotors is the spend-no-more-than-needed option at about $115. Akebono ceramic pads are the quietest available but cost more — fair tradeoff if you daily-drive the YJ. Avoid the no-name $30 rotor kits on eBay; they warp inside a year and the pad material doesn't bed properly.
steps: Loosen lug nuts while wheel is on the ground.
Jack up the front and set on jack stands under the frame rail forward of the leaf spring eye.
Remove the wheel.
Remove brake fluid from master cylinder reservoir (suck out ~1/3 with a turkey baster).
Remove the two 13mm caliper slide bolts on the back of the caliper.
Lift caliper off the bracket; hang it from the spring with wire — DO NOT let it dangle from the hose.
Pull old pads from the bracket (note position of any wear-indicator clip — it goes on the inboard pad).
Compress the piston with a C-clamp and the old inboard pad as a backer.
Wire-brush the bracket where pads slide; apply thin film of anti-seize to slide pins and pad-contact points on the bracket.
Install new pads. Apply anti-seize to slide bolts; reinstall caliper; torque slide bolts to 25 ft-lbs.
To replace rotors: remove the two 17mm bracket-to-knuckle bolts; lift the bracket off; slide rotor off the hub.
Wire-brush the hub face clean. Install new rotor.
Reinstall bracket; torque bracket bolts to 100 ft-lbs.
Repeat opposite side.
Refill master cylinder to MAX line. Pump pedal 5–10 times until firm.
Reinstall wheels, torque lug nuts to 80 ft-lbs in star pattern.
Drive at 10–15 mph and perform 5 firm (not panic) stops from 30 mph to bed pads.
pros: Standard floating-caliper design — same procedure as most American 4x4s of the era.
Z16 pad-and-rotor kit replaces both wear items at once for under $130.
Front brakes do 70% of stopping work; this is the highest-payoff brake maintenance you can do.
cons: 1987–1989 vs 1990+ rotor/caliper sizes don't interchange; verify your year before ordering.
Caliper slide pins on neglected trucks corrode in their bores — plan for time and PB Blaster if your truck has sat outdoors.
Soft brake pedal after the job usually means air entered the line during piston compression; bleed if pedal doesn't firm up.

title: Budget Trail YJ — 4-Inch Lift, 33s, and Lockers Done Right
skills_required: planning a build in the right order

parts.name: Suspension lift (3-4 in spring or spring-over) + shocks
Rear locker (selectable or lunchbox) for Dana 35/44

citations.title: Jeep YJ build planning — lift, tire, gear math references
Spring-over vs spring lift for leaf-sprung YJ (Pirate4x4 tech)

summary: A YJ is one of the best-value trail platforms you can build: short, light, solid-axle, and leaf-sprung, so it gets to 33s cheaply. The sane budget recipe is a 3-4 inch lift, 33x12.5R15 tires, a rear locker, a slip-yoke eliminator with a CV driveshaft, and a regear to 4.56 — in that order. Plan on $2,500-$6,000 depending on how much you do yourself and whether you regear. The mistake to avoid is bolting on big tires and a tall lift first and dealing with the driveline vibration, weak Dana 35, and lost gearing as afterthoughts.
description:
The YJ's leaf-sprung suspension and light weight are exactly what make it cheap to build. You do not need coilovers and long arms; you need the right springs, the driveline corrections a lift demands, and a plan that spends money in the order that actually improves the Jeep. Here is the build that works without wasting money.

For 33s, a **3-4 inch lift** clears them with minor trimming. You have two paths: a conventional **spring lift** (new taller leaf packs and longer shackles, simplest and most comfortable on-road) or a **spring-over axle (SOA)** conversion, which is cheap flex but raises the center of gravity and needs care with steering geometry and driveline angles. For most people a quality spring lift plus good shocks is the right call; SOA is for those chasing maximum articulation who will address the geometry. Run **33x12.5R15** on 15-inch wheels for the cheapest strong tire/wheel combo.

A 4-inch YJ lift breaks two things you must fix: **driveline angle** and **gearing**. Add a **slip-yoke eliminator and CV rear driveshaft** to cure the vibration, and set the rear pinion angle to the new geometry. Then **regear to 4.56** so 33s feel like stock tires did — the YJ's factory 3.55/3.73 gears leave the engine gutless on 33s. Skipping the regear is the most common "why is my built YJ so slow" complaint.

Add a **rear locker** first — it is the single biggest capability upgrade for the money, and a selectable or lunchbox locker drops into the Dana 35 or 44. But know the **Dana 35 is the weak link**: it survives 33s with a locker if you drive smart, but hard use or 35s will break axle shafts. Budget for shaft upgrades or a Dana 44 swap if you push it. A front locker or limited-slip comes later, after the rear.

Do it in this order: lift + shocks, tires/wheels, SYE + driveshaft, rear locker, regear, then armor and a front locker. Spending in this sequence means each step works with the last instead of needing redone. Get an alignment after the lift and steering work, and re-torque everything after a shakedown run.
pros: The cheapest credible path to a real 33-inch trail rig
Leaf-sprung and light, so the YJ needs no exotic suspension
Build-order plan avoids the classic redo-it-twice money pit
cons: The Dana 35 limits you — plan around it or upgrade it
A 4-inch lift mandates the SYE/driveshaft and regear, not optional
SOA is cheap flex but raises center of gravity — choose carefully

title: AX-15 Manual Transmission Service — YJ (and the BA-10 Problem)
skills_required: clutch/transmission R&R for a swap or reseal

parts.name: Manual transmission fluid (AX-15: 75W-90 GL-3 or Mopar spec)

citations.title: Novak Conversions — AX-15 transmission reference (Jeep)
Jeep YJ factory service manual — manual transmission fluid spec

summary: The AX-15 is the good 5-speed behind the YJ 4.0L — a stout Aisin-built box that lives a long life on the right fluid and a working shifter. If you have an early (1987-1989) 4.2L or 4.0L YJ with the **Peugeot BA-10/5**, that transmission is the weak one, and the AX-15 is the standard, near-bolt-in upgrade. A fluid service is $40 and an hour; a BA-10-to-AX-15 swap is a weekend and a few hundred dollars in parts. Use the correct manual-trans fluid — the AX-15 hates the wrong oil and will notch into second when cold if you feed it the wrong stuff.
description:
Jeep used two very different transmissions behind the bigger YJ engines. The 1987-1989 trucks often got the **BA-10/5**, a Peugeot unit that is fragile and parts-scarce. From 1989 on, the **AX-15** (a Toyota/Aisin design) became the manual behind the 4.0L, and it is one of the better light-duty Jeep transmissions ever fitted. Knowing which you have decides whether you are doing maintenance or planning a swap.

The AX-15 is sensitive to fluid. The factory called for a specific GL-3 gear oil; many owners run a synchromesh-type manual transmission fluid (such as Pennzoil Synchromesh) for smoother cold shifts. Avoid heavy GL-5 hypoid gear oil — it can attack the synchros and the yellow-metal parts. Pull the fill plug first (if it will not come out, do not drain — you would be stuck), then the drain plug, and refill to the fill-hole level. A notchy second-gear shift when cold is the classic "wrong fluid" symptom and a fluid change often cures it.

If your YJ still has the BA-10/5, plan for it to fail and budget the AX-15 swap. The AX-15 bolts to the same 4.0L bellhousing pattern and mates to the NP207/NP231 transfer case, so the swap is mostly a matter of sourcing a good used AX-15, the matching clutch and bellhousing, and the correct shifter. It is the established, well-documented fix and turns a fragile driveline into a durable one. Source a unit from a 4.0L donor for the right input and gearing.

A vague or rattly shifter is usually worn shifter bushings and the shift-tower components, not the transmission internals — rebuild the shifter before condemning the box. While the transmission is out for a reseal or swap, do the clutch, rear main seal, and pilot bearing as a set; you do not want to pull it twice. Refill, bleed the hydraulics if equipped, and verify clean engagement in all gears.
pros: The AX-15 is durable and well-supported — a fluid service goes a long way
A BA-10-to-AX-15 swap permanently fixes the weak early driveline
Correct fluid cures the common cold-shift notchiness for cheap
cons: Wrong fluid (GL-5 hypoid) damages synchros — read the spec
A full swap is a weekend job with clutch and sourcing involved
BA-10 parts are scarce; do not pour money into rebuilding one

title: Slip-Yoke Eliminator and CV Driveshaft — YJ (NP231)

citations.title: Tom Woods Driveshafts — SYE and CV driveshaft tech (Jeep NP231)
JB Conversions SYE installation instructions (NP231)

summary: Once a YJ goes past about a 3-4 inch lift, the NP231's long factory slip-yoke driveshaft runs at too steep an angle and you get a vibration you cannot tune out. A slip-yoke eliminator (SYE) plus a double-cardan (CV) rear driveshaft fixes it at the source by shortening the tailhousing and letting the driveshaft operate at the correct compound angle. Budget $350-$800 for the kit and a custom-length shaft. This is the upgrade that makes a lifted YJ smooth again — skip it and you will chase driveline vibration forever.
description:
The NP231 transfer case used in 1988-1995 YJs has a slip-yoke output: the driveshaft slides in and out of a long tailhousing. At stock height it works fine, but lift the Jeep and the rear pinion angle changes, putting the single-joint slip-yoke shaft at a steep operating angle that vibrates and wears U-joints fast. The SYE replaces the slip output with a fixed yoke, and a CV driveshaft handles the steeper angle with a double-cardan joint at the transfer-case end.

A standard driveshaft U-joint wants its operating angle matched at both ends, within a few degrees. Lift the YJ and you cannot satisfy that with the long factory slip-yoke shaft — you either get vibration or you rotate the pinion up so far that the slip-yoke binds. The SYE + CV combination breaks that compromise: the CV joint at the t-case end absorbs the angle, and you point the rear pinion straight at the CV joint instead of parallel to the driveshaft. It is the correct fix, not a band-aid.

Drain the transfer case and support it. The SYE kit replaces the rear output shaft, bearing, and tailhousing — most kits are a "short" SYE that also shortens the case by a couple of inches (buying back driveshaft length). Follow the kit's order for pressing the speedometer/tone components and setting the snap ring. Torque the tailhousing bolts to spec, refill with the specified fluid, and check for leaks. Take careful measurements for the driveshaft after the SYE is in — the shaft is built to your exact pinion-to-yoke length.

With the SYE installed, set the rear axle pinion to point at the transfer-case CV joint (not parallel to the shaft) — a degree shim under the leaf springs or adjusting your lift's pinion correction gets you there. Measure center-to-center for the CV driveshaft and order it built to length. After install, test drive and check for vibration across the speed range; a remaining vibration usually means the pinion angle needs a small shim change.
pros: Permanently cures lifted-YJ driveline vibration at the source
Fixed yoke is stronger and seals better than the slip output
Lets you run a proper pinion angle without slip-yoke bind
cons: Requires opening the transfer case — more involved than a bolt-on
The CV driveshaft is a custom-length part, not off-the-shelf
Pinion angle must be set correctly or the vibration persists

title: 4.2L 258 to 4.0L HO Swap — What It Takes (YJ)

parts.name: Donor 4.0L HO engine + harness + PCM (1991-1995 YJ/XJ)
Motor mounts / adapter for 4.0L in YJ
Fuel system: return-style pump, lines, regulator
Radiator, exhaust, and accessory brackets to suit 4.0L

citations.title: Novak Conversions — AMC 4.0L into Jeep swap reference
NAXJA / Jeep forums — 258 to 4.0L HO swap writeups

summary: Swapping the carbureted 4.2L 258 for a fuel-injected 4.0L HO is the single biggest drivability upgrade for an early YJ: more power, far better cold starts, modern fuel injection, and a stronger AX-15 behind it if you swap the trans too. It is a real project — 20 to 60 hours and $800-$4,000 depending on how complete your donor is — but the parts share a family lineage, so it bolts in more cleanly than most engine swaps. The make-or-break detail is the wiring: do the harness and PCM integration right and the rest is mechanical.
description:
The AMC 258 (4.2L) is a torquey, durable engine, but in carbureted YJ form it is down on power and finicky in the cold and at altitude. The 4.0L HO that replaced it (1991+) makes about 180 hp with sequential fuel injection and starts instantly in any weather. Because both are AMC inline-sixes sharing the same basic block architecture and bellhousing pattern, the 4.0L drops into the YJ engine bay with known mounts and mates to Jeep transmissions.

The cleanest path is a complete 1991-1995 4.0L HO donor from a YJ or XJ: engine, the full engine wiring harness, the PCM, and the fuel-injection components. Buying these as a matched set from one vehicle saves enormous headaches versus assembling piecemeal. A YJ donor is ideal because the accessory layout and motor mounts match your chassis most closely. Inspect the donor for the renowned 0331 head-crack issue before you buy.

The 258 is carbureted, so your YJ has no fuel-injection harness or computer. You will integrate the 4.0L engine harness and PCM, add a return-style fuel system (an injected engine needs supply and return plus the right pressure), and sort out the ignition, sensors, and gauges. This is where swaps succeed or fail — take your time labeling and routing the harness, and use a known-good donor PCM matched to the engine and transmission type.

Plan for a 4.0L-spec radiator (the injected engine and its electric fan setup differ from the carb truck), the correct exhaust manifold and downpipe, and accessory brackets that match the 4.0L. If you are also moving to the AX-15 (recommended over a BA-10), do the clutch, bellhousing, and crossmember in the same project. Set motor mounts and pinion/driveline angles, then commission the fuel and ignition systems carefully on first start.
pros: Huge gain in power, cold-start, and all-around drivability
Family-shared architecture makes it a relatively clean swap
Pairs naturally with the stronger AX-15 transmission upgrade
cons: Big time investment and a real budget, especially if the donor is incomplete
Wiring/PCM integration is the hard part — not a weekend job
Needs fuel-system, cooling, and exhaust changes, not only the engine

title: Hard-Start / No-Start Diagnosis — YJ 4.0L, 4.2L, and RENIX
tools_required: noid light or injector test light

citations.title: International Full Size Jeep / 4.0L tech — crank position sensor no-start
RENIX vs HO 4.0L diagnosis reference (NAXJA tech)

summary: A YJ that cranks but will not start is almost always a spark, fuel, or sensor problem with a short list of usual suspects — and on the fuel-injected 4.0L, the **crankshaft position sensor (CPS)** is the number-one cause of a no-start or intermittent hot-start. Diagnose in order: confirm spark, confirm fuel pressure, then check the CPS and grounds before buying anything. The work is mostly free with a multimeter; the fix is usually a $40-$120 sensor. Resist the parts-cannon — a YJ no-start rewards a methodical spark-fuel-air check.
description:
YJs came with three very different fuel/ignition setups: the carbureted **4.2L 258**, the **RENIX** fuel-injected 4.0L (1987-1990), and the **HO** 4.0L (1991-1995) with the more familiar Chrysler injection. The diagnostic order is the same for all three — spark, then fuel, then the sensor and grounds — but where you look differs by system.

Pull a plug wire, fit a spark tester, and crank. **No spark** on the injected 4.0L points hard at the **crankshaft position sensor** (mounted at the bellhousing, reading the flywheel) — a failing CPS is the classic "ran fine, now cranks and won't start, especially when hot" complaint. Check the CPS connector and resistance against spec before condemning it. On the carbureted 258, no spark sends you to the ignition module, coil, and the pickup in the distributor. Weak or intermittent spark on any of them often traces to corroded grounds — the YJ's engine and body grounds are a common root cause.

On the injected engines, key on and listen for the in-tank pump prime; put a gauge on the fuel rail and verify pressure to spec (and that it holds). No prime points at the pump, relay, or ASD circuit. A noid light at the injector connector confirms the injectors are being pulsed. On the carbureted 258, check that the mechanical pump delivers fuel and that the carburetor is not flooded or dry.

If spark and fuel both check out but it still will not start, suspect the CPS (injected) or the ignition pickup (carb), and clean every engine-to-body and battery ground — RENIX 4.0L systems in particular are famously sensitive to ground quality and will throw odd no-start and stalling behavior when grounds are corroded. Refresh the grounds at the head, the firewall, and the battery before chasing ghosts. Only after spark, fuel, and grounds are verified should you look at the ECU or wiring harness.
pros: A clear spark-then-fuel-then-sensor order solves most YJ no-starts fast
The likely fix (CPS or a ground refresh) is cheap
Most of the diagnosis costs nothing but a multimeter and time
cons: Three different systems (carb / RENIX / HO) need slightly different checks
A hot-only no-start (CPS) can fool you by restarting once cooled
Corroded grounds mimic sensor and ignition failures — check them early
This is a diagnostic guide; on a YJ you may also be chasing it on the trail, so carry a spare CPS once you have confirmed it as your weak point.

title: Serpentine Belt Replacement

parts.name: Goodyear Gatorback Poly-V belt (4.0L w/ AC)
Mopar belt tensioner (later YJ w/ tensioner)

citations.title: 4.0L serpentine belt routing — getahelmet.com
YJ 2.5L/4.0L tensioner bolt — eBay listing

summary: The YJ 4.0L runs a single serpentine belt around the crank, water pump, alternator, power steering, AC, and (on some years) a tensioner pulley. Plan on 30 minutes for the swap, longer if it's your first time figuring out the routing on an AC-equipped truck.
description:
The 1991–1995 YJ 4.0L uses a Poly-V serpentine belt that drives every accessory off the crankshaft. The 4.2L 258 in 1987–1990 uses an older multi-belt setup with V-belts for AC, alternator, and power steering — this guide covers both, but the serpentine belt swap on the 4.0L is the more common job. **Goodyear Gatorback 4060882** (or the Gates equivalent **K060882**) is the right belt for AC-equipped 4.0L trucks. Non-AC trucks run a shorter belt; check the parts catalog by your specific configuration before ordering.

Belt tensioning on the YJ varies by year and accessory layout. Some 4.0L YJs run a spring-loaded automatic tensioner; others use a manual adjustment where you loosen the power steering pump bracket and pry the pump outward against a slot. **Take a photo of the existing belt routing before you remove anything** — the routing diagram under the hood is often faded or missing on a 30-year-old Jeep, and routing the new belt incorrectly will overheat the engine within minutes if the water pump spins backward.

Inspect the pulleys with the belt off. The water pump pulley should spin smoothly with no roughness or play. Power steering and alternator bearings should feel the same. A whining or growling bearing means you're going back in within a few months — replace it now while the belt is off. Check the tensioner pulley if equipped; a dry bearing or sloppy arm will eat belts.

Install the new belt by routing it around every pulley except the smoothest accessory (usually power steering or the tensioner pulley) last. Apply tension, double-check that every groove is fully seated in every pulley, and start the engine for 30 seconds. The belt should track straight without squealing. A new belt sometimes chirps for the first few minutes — if it persists, your routing is wrong or a pulley is misaligned.
steps: Photograph the current belt routing; download the FSM diagram for backup.
Locate the tensioner (automatic) or adjustment bolt (manual on power steering).
Rotate the tensioner with a 1/2-inch breaker bar to slacken the belt; on manual setups, loosen the pump bracket and pry inward.
Slip the belt off the smoothest pulley first; remove from each accessory.
Spin every pulley by hand — replace anything rough or noisy now.
Route the new belt to match your photo; seat fully in every groove.
Reapply tension; on auto-tensioner, let it self-tension; on manual, set deflection per FSM (about 1/2-inch at the longest run).
Start the engine for 30 seconds; verify the belt tracks straight and pulleys spin true.
Reinspect tension after 100 miles of driving — new belts stretch.
pros: One belt drives every accessory on the 4.0L — far more straightforward than the 258's multi-belt setup.
Aftermarket Gates and Goodyear belts cost $25–$30 and last 60,000 miles.
Catches dying bearings before they strand you.
cons: AC-equipped trucks have tight clearance around the compressor — knuckle skin is at risk.
Routing diagrams under the hood are often faded; photograph before disassembly.
Mismatched belt length (AC vs non-AC) is the most common ordering mistake.

title: Brake Fluid Flush

citations.title: AutoZone — YJ Bleeding Brake System
Brake fluid flush procedure — Wrangler TJ Forum (same architecture)

summary: The YJ uses DOT 3 brake fluid. Flush every two years or 30,000 miles in the order furthest-from-master-cylinder first: passenger rear → driver rear → passenger front → driver front. The whole job takes about an hour with a helper.
description:
Brake fluid is hygroscopic — it absorbs water from the atmosphere through the seals, master cylinder cap, and flex hoses. Water-saturated fluid boils at a lower temperature, which means pedal fade during long descents, and it corrodes the inside of every steel brake line, caliper bore, and wheel cylinder. The YJ's brake system is unsophisticated (no ABS, no proportioning valve drama) but every component is steel or cast iron, so neglected fluid eats the system from the inside out. Flush every two years and the master cylinder, calipers, and wheel cylinders will outlive the truck.

DOT 3 is the factory spec. DOT 4 is acceptable as an upgrade — it has a higher dry boiling point and the same chemistry, so it mixes cleanly with existing DOT 3. Do not use DOT 5 silicone fluid; it is not compatible with DOT 3/4 systems and will destroy the seals. Stick with DOT 3 from any major brand (Valvoline, Prestone, Wagner) and you're fine. Two 32-ounce bottles is enough for a full flush with margin.

The bleeding sequence on a YJ is the same as any non-ABS truck: **start at the wheel furthest from the master cylinder and work back**. That's passenger-side rear first, then driver-side rear, then passenger-side front, then driver-side front. The rear wheels use wheel cylinders with the bleeder on top; the fronts use caliper bleeders also on top. Every bleeder is 10mm. Crack each one before you raise the truck — frozen bleeders are common, and breaking one off means a wheel cylinder or caliper replacement.

The two-person method is: helper pumps the pedal three times slowly and holds; you open the bleeder, watch fluid jet out, close before the pedal hits the floor; helper releases. Repeat until clean fluid runs and no air bubbles come out. **Keep the master cylinder reservoir at least three-quarters full the entire time** — let it run dry and you'll pull air into the master, doubling the job. Suction the old fluid out of the reservoir with a turkey baster before you start to speed the flush.
steps: Crack all four bleeder screws before raising the truck; replace any that won't break loose.
Suction old fluid out of the master cylinder reservoir with a turkey baster.
Refill master cylinder with fresh DOT 3 to the upper mark.
Attach clear tubing to passenger-rear bleeder; submerge other end in catch bottle.
Helper pumps brake pedal three times slowly, holds firm; open bleeder, watch fluid, close before pedal bottoms; helper releases.
Repeat at passenger-rear until clean fluid runs clear with no bubbles (3–5 cycles typical).
Top off master cylinder; move to driver-rear, then passenger-front, then driver-front, repeating step 5–6.
Final check: pedal should be firm; test in driveway before road test.
Recheck fluid level after first 20 miles; top up if needed.
pros: $15 of fluid prevents $300 of corroded caliper rebuilds down the road.
DOT 4 is a no-downside upgrade for towing or desert driving.
Doing this every two years means the master cylinder, calipers, and wheel cylinders likely outlive the truck.
cons: Old bleeders strip or snap on neglected trucks — budget for replacements before tearing into a 30-year-old system.
Letting the master cylinder run dry doubles the job; stay disciplined with refills.
DOT 5 silicone fluid is a one-way trip — never put it in a system that's seen DOT 3.

title: Coolant Flush — 4.0L and 258

citations.title: Mishimoto YJ/TJ racing thermostat application
Quadratec 1987-1995 YJ cooling system

summary: Open the petcock at the bottom of the radiator, drain into a pan, refill with a 50/50 mix of distilled water and full-strength antifreeze, run with the heater on max to bleed air, and top off — total system capacity is about 10 quarts.
description:
YJ cooling systems are old enough that the original coolant has been in the truck longer than most readers have owned the truck. Antifreeze breaks down chemically over time — the corrosion inhibitors deplete first, then the dielectric properties — and used coolant becomes mildly acidic, which eats heater cores, head gaskets, and water pumps from the inside. A coolant flush every three years or 36,000 miles is the cheapest preventative you can do.

The system holds **10 quarts (2.5 gallons)** on a 4.0L and slightly less on a 4.2L 258 — figure two gallons of pre-mixed 50/50 plus an extra gallon for top-off. The factory specified the green ethylene glycol — Prestone, Peak, or Zerex are all fine. Avoid mixing colors (orange Dex-Cool, gold, etc.) because the chemistries fight each other and form a gel. Always use distilled water if you mix your own — tap water deposits minerals on the inside of the head and radiator over time.

The thermostat is a 195°F unit and lives under the housing at the front of the head. While you have the system drained, swap it. Replace the housing gasket at the same time — they cost $6 and are the most common leak point after a thermostat job. Torque the housing bolts to **17 ft-lbs**; over-torquing cracks the cast housing. If the original housing is corroded or has cracks around the bolt holes, replace it now with a Mopar or Crown aluminum housing. Plastic aftermarket housings warp under heat and are not worth the savings.

Bleeding air is the step most people get wrong. Park the truck nose-up on a hill or ramps so the radiator cap is the highest point in the system. Refill with the cap off, start the engine, set the heater to maximum heat with the fan on low, and let it warm up until the upper radiator hose is hot. The thermostat opens, the air burps out, the coolant level drops — top it off. Squeeze the upper hose a few times to help. Cap on, drive around the block, let it cool overnight, recheck level in the overflow bottle in the morning.
steps: Cold engine. Place 3+ gallon drain pan under radiator petcock (driver-side bottom of radiator).
Open petcock with channel-locks; let radiator drain.
Drain block: remove the block drain plug (passenger side of block, 1/2" pipe plug) — catches another 2–3 quarts.
Close drains. Optional: fill with water + flush product, run to temp, drain again.
Remove thermostat housing; clean mating surface; install new thermostat (spring side toward engine) with new gasket.
Torque housing bolts to 17 ft-lbs.
Park nose-up on ramps. Fill radiator and overflow bottle with 50/50 distilled water + antifreeze.
Start engine, heat on max, fan on low, cap off.
Run until upper hose is hot and thermostat opens. Top off radiator as level drops.
Cap on, drive around the block, cool overnight, recheck overflow level in morning.
pros: Renews corrosion protection — single biggest cause of YJ head gasket failures is depleted coolant.
Forced opportunity to inspect hoses, clamps, and water pump weep hole.
Combines well with a thermostat replacement; both share the same drain step.
cons: Air bleeding is fiddly; expect to top off three or four times over the first few drives.
Heater core can air-lock and stay cold even after radiator is full — squeeze upper hose and rev to clear.
Used coolant is toxic to pets and wildlife — keep the drain pan covered and dispose at a recycling center.

title: Differential Fluid Change — Dana 30, Dana 35, Dana 44

citations.title: TJ Forum — Dana 30 and Dana 35 fluid change capacities
Motobilt — Wrangler differential fluid capacity chart

summary: Pull the cover, drain, scrape the old RTV clean, lay a 1/8" bead of new RTV around the cover flange, torque cover bolts in star pattern, and refill through the fill plug until oil dribbles out — Dana 30 takes about 1 quart, Dana 35 takes 2 quarts, Dana 44 takes about 3 quarts.
description:
Differential fluid is one of those services that's invisible until it kills the axle. The oil sees high heat, fine metal particles from normal gear wear, and water intrusion if you ford streams or wash with a pressure washer. Change interval is 30,000 miles for street driving, 15,000 miles or annually for trail use, and immediately after any water crossing where you suspect the axle vent ingested water (cloudy or milky oil = water contamination — change it now or lose the carrier bearings).

YJ axle math: the front is a **Dana 30** on every YJ, about 1 quart capacity. The rear is a **Dana 35** on 4-cylinder and most 6-cylinder YJs (~2 quarts), or an optional **Dana 44** on a small number of trucks (~3 quarts). If your rear cover has 10 bolts and a flat-bottom shape, it's a Dana 35. If it has 10 bolts but a more rounded shape and is noticeably larger, it's a Dana 44. Check the tag on the cover or the casting if you're unsure.

The Dana 30 has a square-headed fill plug at the front-passenger side of the housing — a 3/8" drive ratchet fits directly into the square hole. The Dana 35 fill plug is a rubber-and-metal stopper that you pry off with a flathead screwdriver. Most YJs don't have a drain plug — you pull the cover to drain. Plan for that: have a new gasket or a tube of RTV, a wire brush to scrape the old sealant, and brake cleaner to degrease the mating surface. Cover bolt torque is **20 ft-lbs** for Dana 30 and Dana 35, **30 ft-lbs** for Dana 44. Tighten in a star pattern in three passes — even pressure prevents cover-flange warp.

Fluid choice: 80W-90 conventional gear oil is the factory spec. 75W-90 synthetic shifts a bit more manageable in cold weather and runs slightly cooler under load — worth the extra $6 per quart on trail-driven rigs. If your rear has the Trac-Lok limited-slip clutch pack (most YJs do not — it was optional), add 4 oz of friction modifier or use a gear oil rated for limited-slip use, or the clutches will chatter on tight turns.

Fill until oil dribbles out the fill hole with the axle level — that's the correct level by design. Over-filling pushes oil past seals and onto your brake drums. Underfilling starves the ring gear and burns the pinion bearing. Both axles have a vent tube on top — pull the vent hose and verify it isn't crushed or plugged before you drive away.
steps: Park on level ground. Loosen fill plug FIRST (verify you can get it out — if it's seized, don't drain the axle).
Position drain pan under differential cover.
Remove all-but-two cover bolts on the upper half of the cover; loosen those two.
Pry cover loose at the bottom with a flathead — oil drains. Catch in pan.
Remove last two bolts; remove cover.
Wipe inside of housing clean. Inspect ring gear and check magnet at bottom of cover (fine fuzz = normal; chunks = stop and rebuild).
Scrape old RTV from cover and housing flanges; degrease with brake cleaner.
Apply 1/8" bead of RTV around cover flange OR install new gasket.
Reinstall cover; torque bolts in star pattern: 20 ft-lbs (D30/D35) or 30 ft-lbs (D44), three passes.
Let RTV cure 1 hour before adding fluid.
Pump fresh gear oil through fill plug until oil dribbles out level.
Reinstall fill plug; torque to 25 ft-lbs (D30/D35) or 35 ft-lbs (D44).
Verify axle vent tube is clear; reattach if disconnected.
Repeat for other axle.
pros: Smallest investment in the longest-life drivetrain component on the truck.
Inspecting the cover magnet on every change catches gear failure months before catastrophic noise.
Synthetic 75W-90 lasts 50% longer than conventional under trail abuse.
cons: No drain plug on the cover means a messy job — paper towels and degreaser everywhere.
Dana 35 is the platform's weakest link; if you find chunks on the magnet, plan an axle upgrade (Dana 44 or Ford 8.8 swap).
RTV cure time of an hour is non-negotiable; rushing fill leaks the cover.

title: Oil Change — 4.0L and AMC 258

citations.title: Mopar 4.0L oil filter 5281090AB
Wrangler YJ oil filter listing

summary: Drop the 13mm drain plug, spin off the filter on the passenger side, refill with 6 quarts of 10W-30 (4.0L) or 5W-30 (4.0L in cold climates), and tighten everything to spec — first oil change on a YJ takes about 30 minutes once you've done it.
description:
The AMC inline-six in the YJ runs forever on clean oil and falls apart on neglected oil. Both engines — the 4.2L 258 (1987–1990) and the 4.0L HO (1991–1995) — share an oil-pan layout, a side-mounted spin-on filter, and a forgiveness for cheap conventional oil if you change it often. The 4.0L holds 6 quarts with filter; the 4.2L 258 holds 5 quarts with filter. Use 10W-30 for desert and summer, 5W-30 if you see freezing temps. Full synthetic is a real upgrade after 100k miles when the rings start letting a little blow-by through.

Mopar's filter for the 1991–1995 4.0L is **5281090AB** (M0-090 on some packaging). The 4.2L 258 takes the older **33004195**. Wix, Bosch, and Mobil 1 all make a fitting alternative — anything with the right thread and gasket size will work, but the Mopar filter has the strongest anti-drainback valve, which matters on a side-mounted filter where oil can siphon back into the pan on shutdown.

Warm the engine for five minutes before draining — warm oil carries more suspended particles out with it. The drain plug on the pan is a 13mm hex head; the torque spec is **22 ft-lbs**. The filter sits horizontal on the passenger side of the block above the starter — a swivel-handle filter wrench or the cap-style wrench made for this filter size makes it manageable from the side. Spin the new filter on by hand until the gasket touches the block, then another three-quarters turn. Don't gorilla it — the gasket does the sealing, not the torque.

After refill, run the engine for 30 seconds, shut it down, wait two minutes, and recheck the dipstick. Top up to the upper mark. Drive it around the block and check for drips at the filter and drain plug. Log the mileage. The AMC six wants fresh oil every 3,000 miles on conventional or 5,000 miles on synthetic — the engine will thank you with another 100,000 miles of service.
steps: Warm engine 5 minutes, then park level on jack stands or ramps.
Position drain pan under the oil pan plug (driver side, rear of pan).
Remove 13mm drain plug; let drain 10–15 minutes until it stops.
Move drain pan under filter (passenger side, above starter); spin filter off counter-clockwise.
Wipe filter mounting surface clean; check old gasket came off with the filter.
Lubricate new filter gasket with fresh oil; hand-tighten until gasket contacts block + 3/4 turn.
Reinstall drain plug; torque to 22 ft-lbs (use a fresh crush washer if your plug uses one).
Refill: 6 qt for 4.0L, 5 qt for 4.2L 258 with filter; start engine for 30 sec; verify no leaks.
Shut off, wait 2 min, recheck dipstick, top to upper mark.
pros: Side-mounted filter is reachable without ramps if you have long arms.
Both AMC sixes tolerate any major-brand 5W-30 or 10W-30.
5,000-mile synthetic intervals work fine on engines under 150k miles.
cons: Side filter drips oil down the starter and onto the crossmember every time — keep paper towels nearby.
Mopar 5281090AB is harder to find than aftermarket equivalents; order ahead.
Crush washer on drain plug should be replaced — many people skip and end up with weeping plugs.

title: Spark Plug Replacement — 4.0L and 258

citations.title: RC12LYC application — 87-98 2.5/4.0L YJ and TJ
Spark plug torque 4.0L discussion

summary: Pull the wires one at a time, swap each Champion RC12LYC (gapped to 0.035") with a dab of anti-seize on the threads, torque to 27 ft-lbs, and call it done in under an hour.
description:
The AMC inline-six is one of the friendliest engines on the planet for a spark plug change. All six plugs sit in a straight line along the passenger side of the head, each one exposed and reachable without removing a thing. The whole job is 30 to 45 minutes the first time, and 20 minutes after that. Plug life on copper Champions is 30,000 miles; platinum aftermarket equivalents can stretch to 60,000 miles but the engine doesn't run any better on them — the HEI-spec ignition on the 4.0L makes great spark either way.

The factory plug is the Champion **RC12LYC** (or **RC12YC** on early YJs) — both interchange. Gap is **0.035"** on engines with the distributor cap (which covers every YJ); set the gap with a feeler gauge or a wire gap tool before installing. NGK and Autolite make crossover plugs that work fine — what matters is the heat range, which is what the 12 designates. Don't run plugs cooler than the OE heat range unless your engine is built; you'll foul them at idle.

Pull one wire at a time and replace one plug at a time — that way you cannot mix up the firing order. The boots get stiff with age; twist before pulling. Use a 5/8" spark plug socket with a rubber insert to hold the plug, and a short extension for clearance under the hood. Apply a small dab of anti-seize on the threads (a thin film, not a glob — too much and the torque reading gets thrown off). Thread by hand for at least three turns to confirm you haven't cross-threaded the aluminum head — this is the most common failure point for a plug change. Torque to **27 ft-lbs**.

While you're in there, look at each old plug as it comes out. White ash = lean, oily black = rich or burning oil, dry black = running rich or short trips. A normal plug pulled from a healthy 4.0L will be tan to light brown. If one plug looks different from the other five, that cylinder has a problem worth chasing.
steps: Cold engine. Pull #1 plug wire (front of engine), twisting at the boot before pulling straight up.
Blow debris out of the plug well with compressed air or by mouth.
Use 5/8" spark plug socket with extension to break the plug loose; spin out by hand.
Inspect old plug; note color and condition.
Set new plug gap to 0.035" with feeler gauge.
Apply thin film of anti-seize to plug threads.
Hand-thread new plug at least 3 turns before tools.
Torque to 27 ft-lbs.
Push wire boot fully onto plug terminal until it clicks.
Repeat for plugs 2 through 6, one at a time.
pros: Straight-line plug layout means every plug is reachable without removing intake or accessories.
$18 set of copper Champions lasts 30,000 miles in normal driving.
Good diagnostic signal — color of old plugs tells you what each cylinder is doing.
cons: Anti-seize gets debated forever online — use a thin film; don't skip it, don't over-apply.
Cross-threading an aluminum head is a several-hundred-dollar repair; always start by hand.
Plug wires aren't included; pair this with a wire-set replacement every other plug change.

title: Transfer Case Fluid — NP207 and NP231

citations.title: NP231 fluid type and capacity — Wrangler Forum
NP-231 transfer case fluid — JeepForum

summary: Both YJ transfer cases — the NP207 (1987–1988) and the NP231 (1988–1995) — use ATF, not gear oil. Drain plug bottom, fill plug side, 2.2 quarts on the NP207, 2.2 quarts on the NP231. The whole job takes about 30 minutes.
description:
The single most common YJ transfer case mistake is dumping 80W-90 into it because it lives next to the differentials that *do* take gear oil. The NP207 and NP231 are both chain-driven, with an internal oil pump that depends on the lighter weight of automatic transmission fluid to circulate. Gear oil starves the pump, the chain wears, and you find out about it when the case starts whining in 4-high. Use ATF.

Either Dexron/Mercon ATF or ATF+4 is acceptable in the NP231 — the chain and synchros aren't fussy. ATF+4 is the modern Mopar spec; Dexron VI works fine and costs less. The earlier NP207 (only in 1987 and very early 1988) was originally spec'd for Dexron II. Use any current Dexron-compatible ATF and you're covered. Capacity for both is roughly 2.2 quarts — but always fill to the **bottom of the fill plug** rather than measuring; that's what "full" means on a transfer case.

The drain and fill plugs on the NP231 are 3/8-inch square — your 3/8-inch ratchet head fits directly into the plug with no socket. The NP207 uses the same square pattern. Crack the **fill plug first** before draining; if you can't get the fill plug out, you can't refill the case, and you do not want that discovery after the case is empty. Once the fill plug breaks loose, remove the drain plug and let it drain into a pan. Dark, smelly fluid is normal. Metal flakes on the magnetic drain plug are normal. Big chunks of metal are not — that's a sign of internal wear and a case rebuild is on the horizon.

Refill until ATF dribbles out of the fill hole, reinstall both plugs with fresh crush washers, torque to **25 ft-lbs**, and drive it. Cycle through 2H, 4H, and 4L on a quiet street and listen — a healthy case is nearly silent. Whining, clunking, or a hard 4L engagement points at chain stretch or worn synchros.
steps: Park level, warm the transfer case (drive 5 minutes), park, and chock the wheels.
Locate fill plug on the driver-side rear of the case; crack it loose first — do not remove yet.
Position drain pan under the lowest point of the case.
Remove drain plug (3/8-inch square); let fully drain (10–15 minutes).
Inspect the magnetic drain plug — light fuzz is normal; chunks mean trouble.
Reinstall drain plug with fresh crush washer; torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Pump ATF into fill hole until it dribbles out of the threads.
Reinstall fill plug; torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Test in 2H, 4H, and 4L; check for leaks at both plugs after 24 hours.
pros: 30-minute job with hand tools — no jack stands required if you can reach under the case.
Square-plug design means no rounded sockets, no stripped Allen heads.
Doing this every 30,000 miles keeps the chain and pump healthy.
cons: ATF dribbles down the crossmember every time — keep paper towels staged.
The fill plug seizes on old jeeps; soak it with PB Blaster the night before.
Commonly confused the transfer case with the transmission below it — verify you're at the rear case before draining.

title: Tie Rod and Drag Link Replacement — YJ
skills_required: setting toe to drive to an alignment

parts.name: Tie rod assembly with new ends (stock or HD)

citations.title: Moog steering and suspension — Jeep YJ tie rod / drag link
Jeep YJ FSM — steering linkage service and torque

summary: Worn tie rod and drag link ends are a top cause of YJ steering wander and a major contributor to front-end wobble — and because they are part of the steering, a failed end means losing steering control. The YJ's linkage is uncomplicated and cheap to replace, and fresh ends transform a vague, darty Jeep into one that tracks straight. Budget $120-$400 depending on stock versus heavy-duty parts, and finish with a professional alignment. You can set toe well enough to drive home, but the Jeep needs a real alignment to wear tires evenly and steer right.
description:
The YJ steers its solid Dana 30 front axle through a tie rod (linking the two wheels) and a drag link (from the steering box to the knuckle). Both use tapered ball-stud ends that wear out with age and trail miles. Loose linkage shows up as on-center wander, a clunk when you change direction, and feathered front tire wear — and on a leaf-sprung short-wheelbase Jeep, worn ends feed directly into the front-end wobble these trucks are prone to.

Lift the front and grab each tire at 3-and-9 o'clock, pushing and pulling with the steering locked: play there points at a tie rod end. Have a helper rock the steering wheel while you watch the drag link and tie rod ends for any lash or a torn boot. A boot that is split has been letting in grit and water, so that joint is worn whether or not it rattles yet. Separate this from ball-joint and wheel-bearing play (felt at 12-and-6) so you fix the right part.

Soak the castle nuts and tapers in penetrating oil. Remove the cotter pin and castle nut, then separate the taper with a tie-rod separator (a pickle fork works but tears the boot, so only fork a part you are replacing). Before removing the old assembly, measure its length or count exposed threads so the new part goes back at the same length, preserving toe well enough to drive. Torque each stud to the service-manual value and install **new** cotter pins — a steering fastener without its cotter pin is a failure waiting to happen.

Set toe close with a tape measure (compare the front-of-tire and rear-of-tire distances) so the Jeep tracks straight, then get a professional alignment to dial toe and verify caster. Correct caster is what gives a solid-axle Jeep its on-center stability and resistance to wobble, so do not skip it — especially on a lifted YJ where lift changes caster. Re-check the fasteners after a few hundred miles, and treat any new looseness or a torn boot as a near-term safety repair.
pros: Restores straight, predictable steering and stops edge tire wear
Cheap, uncomplicated linkage — a high-value safety repair for the money
Removes a primary contributor to YJ front-end wobble
cons: A failed steering end is a genuine safety hazard — do not defer it
Separating tapers cleanly needs the right tool to save good boots
A home toe-set gets you driving; a real alignment is non-negotiable

title: Steering Wander and Front-End Wobble

citations.title: NAXJA / YJ steering tech threads
Moog YJ steering catalog

summary: A leaf-sprung YJ does not get the violent track-bar death wobble that coil Jeeps do — it has no front track bar. What it gets is steering wander, a loose on-center feel, and a shimmy over washboard, and the cause is almost always worn tie-rod ends, a tired steering box, or out-of-balance tires. Check those three before you spend a dollar.
description:
The honest answer: most YJ steering complaints trace to slop in the linkage, not the suspension. With the front wheels off the ground, grab each front tire at 9 and 3 and push-pull — play there is a tie-rod end or the steering box sector shaft. Then grab at 12 and 6 — play there is a wheel bearing or ball joint. A helper turning the wheel while you watch the steering box pitman arm will show sector-shaft lash; the YJ box has an adjustment screw on top, but if it needs more than a small nudge the box is worn out and a reman unit is the real fix.

Tires matter more than YJ owners expect. A single out-of-round or unbalanced 31–33" tire will set up a shimmy that feels like a front-end problem. Rebalance (and road-force balance if a shop has the machine) before condemning parts. Worn leaf-spring bushings and loose spring shackles also let the axle walk under braking — check the shackle bolts and the bushing eyes.

A steering stabilizer is a damper, not a cure. It will quiet a mild shimmy, but if you are relying on it to mask wander, you are hiding a worn part that will eventually let go. Fix the linkage first, then add a quality stabilizer for the last 10 percent.
steps: Lift the front, support on jack stands under the frame, and check linkage play at 9-and-3 and ball joints/bearings at 12-and-6.
Inspect the drag link and tie-rod ends for torn boots and movement; replace any with play.
Check steering box mounting bolts and sector-shaft lash; adjust lightly or replace a worn box.
Rebalance the front tires (road-force if possible) and inspect leaf bushings and shackle bolts.
Only after the above, fit a quality steering stabilizer.

title: YJ Front and Rear Leaf Spring Service

parts.name: Old Man Emu stock-height YJ front leaf pack
Rough Country 2.5" lift YJ leaf pack (front pair)
U-bolt kit (front pair, fits stock-height YJ)

citations.title: Wrangler YJ Suspension Torque Specs — ExtremeTerrain
YJ leaf spring torque thread — JeepForum

summary: A YJ leaf pack lasts 100,000 miles if you're lucky, less if it's lived in the rust belt. Sagging springs, broken main leaves, and snapped center pins all warrant replacement. Plan on a full day for both axles, half a day for one. Torque the u-bolts to 90 ft-lbs; everything else gets torqued with the wheels on the ground.
description:
The YJ runs leaf springs front and rear — five-leaf packs that double as both spring and axle locator. When they sag, ride height drops, caster angle drifts out of spec, and steering goes vague. When the center pin snaps, the axle walks rearward on the spring and your driveshaft angles change in a hurry. Bushings dry out and squeak. If your YJ has 150,000 miles or has lived through more than two desert summers, the springs are probably tired.

Stock-height replacements from Old Man Emu (OME) or BDS will give you back factory ride height with fresh bushings and a controlled rate. If you've been planning a 2.5-inch or 4-inch lift, do the springs and the lift in the same job — replacing leaves twice in a year is wasted work. Rough Country, Skyjacker, and BDS all make YJ-specific kits. Avoid mystery aftermarket "lift springs" from auction sites; the steel quality and arch consistency between pairs is unpredictable.

The factory torque spec is **u-bolts: 90 ft-lbs, shackle bolts: 95 ft-lbs, main eye bolts: 105 ft-lbs, crossmember bolts: 30 ft-lbs**. Some installers torque u-bolts to 70–80 ft-lbs out of fear of bending the spring plates — the factory plates are stamped steel and the 90 ft-lbs spec assumes them. Heavier aftermarket plates handle the full 90 ft-lbs with no complaint. **U-bolts can be torqued at any time. Shackle bolts and main eye bolts must be torqued with the full weight of the vehicle on the ground**, or the bushing seats compress to one position and bind through suspension travel.

The hardest part of the job is breaking loose 30-year-old shackle bolts. Soak every bolt with PB Blaster the night before, then heat with a torch if needed. Cutting the bolts and replacing with greaseable hardware is often faster than fighting them out intact. Greaseable bolts also make future bushing service trivial. Plan for a $40 hardware budget on top of the spring cost.
steps: Soak every shackle and main eye bolt with penetrating oil the day before.
Park level, chock the wheels, raise the frame and support on jack stands.
Support the axle with a floor jack — do not let it hang from brake lines.
Remove the lower shock mount.
Remove u-bolts (4 nuts per spring, 21mm typical).
Remove shackle bolts (rear of spring) and main eye bolt (front of spring).
Pull the spring; transfer the center-pin alignment to the new spring if needed.
Install the new spring: main eye first, then shackle, then position the axle on the spring pin and snug u-bolts.
Torque u-bolts to 90 ft-lbs (or per spring manufacturer's spec for aftermarket plates).
Reinstall the shock; lower the truck to the ground.
With full weight on the wheels, torque shackle bolts to 95 ft-lbs and main eye bolts to 105 ft-lbs.
Recheck all u-bolt torques after 500 miles — new springs settle and u-bolts loosen.
pros: Factory ride height and predictable handling come back overnight.
Greaseable hardware ends the squeak-and-replace cycle for the rest of the truck's life.
Single-job opportunity to upgrade lift height if you've been considering it.
cons: Rusty shackle bolts can turn a half-day job into a two-day fight.
Cheap aftermarket springs vary 1/2-inch side-to-side in arch — measure the new pair before installation.
Suspension geometry shifts will throw caster out of spec; budget for a degreed shim kit if you lift.

title: Shock Replacement — Stock and Lift Heights

citations.title: Bilstein 5100 3–4" YJ front shock — ExtremeTerrain
Bilstein 5100 3–4" YJ shock kit — suspensionlifts.com

summary: Stock-height YJ runs Bilstein 4600 or Rancho RS5000 in factory length. A 2.5-inch lift runs a slightly longer shock; a 3–4-inch lift wants the Bilstein 5100 with 28.44-inch extended / 16.97-inch collapsed travel. Match shock length to lift height — too short bottoms the shaft, too long limits droop.
description:
The YJ uses four shocks — eye-loop on the bottom and a stem with two nuts on the top. They're straightforward to access, straightforward to swap, and probably worn out on any YJ that hasn't had them replaced in the last 80,000 miles. A worn shock won't pass a "park-the-truck and shove the corner downward" bounce test: if the truck oscillates more than one and a half times before settling, the shock is shot.

Bilstein 4600 monotube is the safe default for a stock-height YJ. Bilstein 5100 is the same valving in a longer body for lifted trucks and gives a noticeable improvement in trail manners. Rancho RS5000X is the budget alternative — softer, more comfortable on-road, less composed at speed. The expensive options (Bilstein 7100, King 2.0, Fox 2.0) only make sense on a built rig that sees triple-digit trail speed; on a daily-driven YJ they're overkill.

Length is the part nobody gets right. A stock YJ front shock is **24.5-inch extended, 14.5-inch collapsed**. A 2.5-inch lift wants roughly **27-inch extended, 16-inch collapsed**. A 4-inch lift wants **28.4-inch extended, 17-inch collapsed** — that's the Bilstein 5100 24-064576. Run a shock that's too short and you'll bottom the shaft on every long droop, which destroys the seal and dumps oil within months. Run too long and you cap suspension travel before the axle is at full extension. Measure your current suspension at full droop (let it hang on the springs only) and order shocks rated for that extended length plus an inch of margin.

The eye-loop bushings deserve a fresh squirt of silicone or rubber lube before final torque. The stem-style upper mount has two nuts — torque the bottom (inner) nut against the shock stem to **35 ft-lbs**, then snug the locking nut on top. Don't over-torque the eye bolts; the rubber bushings should compress only slightly when you tighten, not deform into the metal sleeve.
steps: Park level, chock wheels, raise the frame, and support on jack stands.
Support the axle with a floor jack to maintain ride height at the eye end.
Remove the upper stem nuts (front uppers are 13mm; rear uppers are 18mm typically).
Remove the lower eye-loop bolt (18mm or 21mm depending on year).
Pull old shock out; inspect bushings on both ends.
Install new shock, upper stem first; thread on inner mount nut by hand.
Insert lower eye-loop bolt with fresh bushings; torque to 50 ft-lbs.
Torque upper stem mount nut to 35 ft-lbs; snug locking nut.
Lower the truck and bounce-test each corner — one and a half oscillations max.
pros: One of the highest-impact suspension upgrades for the dollar — $300 of shocks transforms a tired YJ.
Eye/stem layout makes the job tool-light: a couple of wrenches and a floor jack.
Can step up later (4600 → 5100 → reservoir shock) without changing mounts.
cons: Frozen upper stem nuts spin the shaft instead of loosening — vise grips on the flat are mandatory.
Wrong-length shock will limit articulation or destroy itself on droop; measure before ordering.
Replacing only the worn pair (front or rear) gives an unbalanced ride — do all four together.

title: Lift Kit Guide: Springs, Shackles, and Spring-Over

citations.title: Rubicon Express YJ application guide
Quadratec YJ suspension catalog

summary: The YJ is leaf-sprung at both ends, which makes lifting it cheaper than any coil Jeep and the geometry forgiving. A 2.5–4 inch spring kit clears 31–33s and bolts in over a weekend. Go past that and a spring-over axle (SOA) is the honest path to 35s — not taller shackles.
description:
Verdict first: full-replacement leaf springs are worth the extra money over add-a-leaf or lift shackles. Add-a-leafs stiffen an already-stiff ride and sag within a year; long shackles change your spring angle and make the truck wander. A quality 2.5–4" spring pack from Rubicon Express, Skyjacker, or Rough Country gives you real travel, predictable handling, and room for 31–33" tires on the stock Dana 30/35 axles.

Whatever the height, budget for the supporting parts. Extended front and rear brake lines are mandatory above 2.5" — stock lines pull tight at full droop and split. A longer or adjustable rear track bar re-centers the axle. Above ~3.5", you are into driveline vibration territory: the rear pinion angle needs shims, and a slip-yoke-eliminator with a CV driveshaft is the proper cure on a lifted YJ, not a transfer-case drop.

For 35s, stop adding lift on top of leaf springs. A spring-over conversion — relocating the springs above the axle instead of below — nets roughly 5–6 inches with flex no shackle lift can match, but it requires new spring perches, a steering correction, and an SYE/CV driveshaft. It is a real fabrication job; plan it as one, or run 33s and call it done.
steps: Lift, support the frame, and remove the wheels; let the axles hang to unload the springs.
Replace springs one corner at a time so the axle stays located; torque U-bolts to spec.
Install extended brake lines and an adjustable rear track bar.
Set rear pinion angle with shims; add an SYE/CV shaft above ~3.5 in.
Re-torque everything after a shakedown drive and re-check alignment (caster/toe).
